subject: Biology
title: The Green Revolution
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Green Revolution usable.

hook.text: In the 1960s, a billion people faced starvation. Plant science helped feed them.

buildup.text: Norman Borlaug bred high-yield, disease-resistant wheat varieties for developing countries.

discovery.text: These dwarf wheat plants put energy into grain instead of tall stems, dramatically boosting harvests.

twist.text: The Green Revolution saved an estimated one billion lives but increased dependence on fertilizers and water.

climax.text: Today's challenge is a second green revolution—feeding 10 billion people sustainably.

punchline.text: A shorter wheat plant saved a billion lives.

quiz.question: What did Norman Borlaug develop during the Green Revolution?

details.summary: The Green Revolution of the 1960s and 1970s introduced high-yield crop varieties, synthetic fertilizers, and irrigation that doubled to tripled grain production worldwide. Led by Norman Borlaug, it saved an estimated billion people from famine while creating environmental challenges.
details.whyItMatters: The Green Revolution demonstrates both the power and consequences of agricultural technology. While averting mass starvation, its reliance on fertilizers and irrigation created dependency, pollution, and biodiversity loss that continue today.
takeaways: Norman Borlaug's dwarf wheat varieties dramatically increased yields in developing countries
Global grain production more than doubled between 1960 and 2000
Environmental costs include groundwater depletion, fertilizer runoff, and reduced crop diversity

faq.question: How did the Green Revolution save a billion lives?
faq.answer: By developing semi-dwarf wheat and rice varieties that channeled more energy into grain rather than tall stalks. Combined with fertilizer and irrigation, yields multiplied. India went from famine risk to food self-sufficiency. Mexico became a wheat exporter.

faq.question: What were the environmental costs of the Green Revolution?
faq.answer: Heavy fertilizer use polluted waterways and created dead zones. Irrigation depleted aquifers. Monoculture replaced diverse traditional varieties, reducing genetic diversity. Pesticide use increased. The social costs included displacement of small farmers unable to afford inputs.
